newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds slip back amid moderate trade.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds slip back amid moderate trade.

text.p: Irish bonds slipped back a little in moderate trade on Thursday in line with an easing of markets generally ahead of key U.S. data due on Friday, dealers said.
Better-than-expected Irish CPI figures for March appeared not to have impacted on the domestic market because "a good result" had already been priced in, dealers said.

"Bonds were well-bid on the back of the numbers but the real significance is that they (the figures) have confirmed Ireland's benign inflation environment and make Irish bond yields very attractive by European standards," one dealer said.

Irish inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, showed a month-on-month rise of 0.1 percent in March, the Central Statistics Office said on Thursday. Most analysts had expected a monthly rise of 0.3 percent.
Dealers said the figures would add to interest in the auction of 150 million Irish pounds of the eight percent Treasury bond due 2006 by the NTMA next Tuesday.

"Irish spreads are narrowing and the 10-year bond is up 15 basis points over the last three weeks," one dealer said. "If the appetite for 10-year bonds in Europe continues, we could see good foreign interest next week."
On Thursday the 10-year spread over bunds in afternoon trading was at 91 basis points, while the five-year pick-up was at 147 basis points.

By 1500 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down six pence from Wednesday's close at 101.57 to yield 6.08 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 15 pence from the close at 107.90 to yield 6.82 percent.
Dealers said that amid continuing worries about the possibility of higher U.S. interest rates, Friday's U.S. data would be the week's key event for markets.

U.S. retail sales data, due at 1230 GMT tomorrow, are forecast to show a 0.6 percent rise in March. Also due are producer prices figures for March, forecast to show unchanged prices on the month for a 1.8 percent year on year rise. -- Kevin Smith, Dublin newsroom + 353 1 661 3377
